Decisions: How to Get Off the Fence
10 Week Psychotherapy Group, In-Person in Beaverton (Canyon Rd)
Lexi Walker, LPC & Natalie Piercy, LPC

Are you facing a decision that feels hard to untangle? If you've been feeling uncertain, overwhelmed, or pulled in different directions, this group is a supportive space to slow down, reflect on your values, and reassess what matters most to you. Through conversation and community, we'll explore personal values, competing priorities, and help you bridge the gap between where you are, and where you want to be.

The Body Keeps the Score book cover
A landmark text on how trauma reshapes both body and brain, and what it takes to recover.

This is one of the books I return to most often — both personally and in my work with clients. Van der Kolk writes with a rare combination of clinical precision and deep compassion, and the result is a book that fundamentally changed how the mental health field understands trauma.

The central argument is deceptively simple: trauma is not just a psychological wound. It lives in the body. The nervous system holds the imprint of overwhelming experiences long after the mind has tried to move on. This is why "just talking about it" often isn't enough — and why so many trauma survivors feel stuck even after years of traditional talk therapy.

Adult Children of Emotionally Immature Parents
Adult Children of Emotionally Immature Parents book cover
A compassionate guide to recognizing emotionally immature parenting and reclaiming your sense of self.

If you've ever felt invisible, overwhelming, or somehow responsible for your parents' emotional wellbeing, this book is likely to feel like someone finally put language to your experience.

Gibson writes clearly and without jargon. She describes emotionally immature parents not as monsters, but as people who — for whatever reason — were never able to tolerate depth, closeness, or their children's authentic needs. The result for adult children is often a deep, quiet loneliness, a tendency to over-function, and a nagging sense that something is wrong with *them* rather than with the dynamic they grew up in.

What I find most clinically useful is how the book helps readers identify their own "role" in the family system — whether they became caretakers, entertainers, or simply learned to disappear. Gibson also offers very practical guidance for how to stop internalizing that old dynamic and start relating to yourself differently.

When the Body Says No book cover
Explores the connection between stress, emotional repression, and physical illness — a must-read for anyone living with chronic health conditions.

The argument is rooted in decades of psychoneuroimmunology research: chronic stress and emotional suppression have measurable effects on the immune and endocrine systems. Maté illustrates this through patient stories that are both deeply specific and utterly universal. You may not share the exact diagnosis, but you will likely recognize the pattern — the person who was always "fine," who took care of everyone else, who learned early that their emotions were inconvenient.

This book has particular resonance for clients navigating autoimmune conditions, fibromyalgia, chronic fatigue, and other illnesses that the medical system often fails to fully address. It's not a book that says illness is your fault — quite the opposite. It's a book that says the circumstances that shaped you had real physiological consequences, and understanding that is part of healing.
